content.text: {"answers":[{"id":"p1","answer":"`define` leaves `auto_attribs=None` and doesn't ask — it tries: `try: return do_it(cls, True) except UnannotatedAttributeError: return do_it(cls, False)`, with the whole class build inside the `try`. SomeClass is fully annotated, so the first attempt (auto_attribs=True) succeeds: `_transform_attrs` reads `_get_annotations(cls)` and loops over the annotations, pulling each name's class-body value out of `cls.__dict__` and wrapping non-`_CountingAttr` values with `attrib(a)`. If the class also had a bare `field()` with no annotation, `_transform_attrs` would compute `unannotated = ca_names - annot_names`, find it non-empty, and raise `UnannotatedAttributeError` naming the offenders — and because that happens at the very top of the build, before the builder has written anything onto the class, `define` cleanly re-enters with `auto_attribs=False`. In that second pass fields come only from `field()`/`attrib()` definitions in the class body (ordered by the `_CountingAttr` counter), so plain annotated assignments like `a_number: int = 42` would no longer be fields at all."},{"id":"p2","answer":"No — SomeClass got no attrs-written `__setattr__` whatsoever. `define`'s `wrap` set `on_setattr = _DEFAULT_ON_SETATTR`, i.e. `setters.pipe(setters.convert, setters.validate)`, and `ClassProps.on_setattr_hook` records it as that `<function pipe.<locals>.wrapped_pipe>`. But in `_ClassBuilder.__init__` the builder scanned both attributes for a non-`None` validator or converter, found neither, and since `self._on_setattr == _DEFAULT_ON_SETATTR and not (has_validator or has_converter)` it set its working copy `self._on_setattr = None` (\"pretend like there's no on_setattr\"). Later `add_setattr` built `sa_attrs` from `a.on_setattr or self._on_setattr`, got an empty set, and returned immediately — so assignment is a plain slot write. The ClassProps record still reports the wrapped_pipe; only the builder's copy was cleared."},{"id":"p3","answer":"`Hashability.UNHASHABLE`. The ladder ran as: `hash` is `None`, `_has_own_attribute(cls, \"__hash__\")` is `False` (the class defines none of its own), `eq` is `True` but `is_frozen` is `False` — so it fell to the final `else`, UNHASHABLE. Consequently `ClassProps.is_hashable` is `False` (true only for `HASHABLE`/`HASHABLE_CACHED`), and `make_unhashable` wrote `self._cls_dict[\"__hash__\"] = None`, so `SomeClass.__hash__` is `None` and `hash(sc)` raises `TypeError`. Note attrs only adds: this `None` shadows, but does not remove, a real `__hash__` on an ancestor."},{"id":"p4","answer":"The generated source is `def __init__(self, a_number=attr_dict['a_number'].default, list_of_numbers=NOTHING):` followed by `self.a_number = a_number` and the factory block. The plain default is referenced indirectly through the `attr_dict` global so the `Attribute` stays the source of truth rather than baking `42` into the text; the factory field's default is the `NOTHING` sentinel. At call time the body runs `if list_of_numbers is not NOTHING: self.list_of_numbers = list_of_numbers else: self.list_of_numbers = __attr_factory_list_of_numbers()`, where `__attr_factory_list_of_numbers` is `list` injected into globals via `_INIT_FACTORY_PAT = \"__attr_factory_%s\"` — so each construction calls `list()` afresh and no two instances share a list. `__init__.__annotations__` is `{'a_number': int, 'list_of_numbers': list[int], 'return': None}`, keyed by alias. Because there is no class- or field-level on_setattr, `_determine_setters` returned the plain `_assign` strategy (bare `self.x = x`, no `_setattr` preamble)."},{"id":"p5","answer":"`attrs.asdict` is a four-line wrapper that forwards to `attr.asdict` with `dict_factory=dict` and `retain_collection_types=True`. `asdict` calls `fields(inst.__class__)` and reads values with `getattr(inst, a.name)`. For `list_of_numbers`, `v = [1,2,3]`, `value_type = list`: not in `_ATOMIC_TYPES`, and `has(list)` is `False` (no `__attrs_attrs__`, `get_generic_base` → None), so the collection branch runs. Since `retain_collection_types=True`, `cf = list`; each element goes through `_asdict_anything`, takes the atomic path and comes back unchanged; then `rv['list_of_numbers'] = cf(items)` **rebuilds a new list object** — so it is *not* the same object as `sc.list_of_numbers` (though it holds the same ints, and the rebuild is shallow, so nested mutables would still be shared). With `attr.asdict`, `retain_collection_types` defaults to `False`, so a tuple- (or set-/frozenset-) valued field would be converted to a `list` instead of being kept as a tuple."},{"id":"p6","answer":"That `__ne__` is not generated code — it is a single shared module-level function in `_make.py` that `add_eq` assigns straight onto the class dict for every attrs class. It computes `result = self.__eq__(other)`; if that is `NotImplemented` it forwards `NotImplemented` unchanged rather than inverting it, otherwise it returns `not result`. Here the generated `__eq__` saw both operands were exactly `SomeClass`, compared `1 == 2`, short-circuited the `and` chain and returned `False`, so `__ne__` returned `True`. Against a non-SomeClass operand, `__eq__`'s `other.__class__ is not self.__class__` guard returns `NotImplemented`, `__ne__` passes it through, and Python falls back to identity comparison."},{"id":"p7","answer":"`make_class` wraps `_attrs` (i.e. `attr.s`), not `define`, so C inherits attr.s's defaults. Differences from SomeClass: (1) `is_slotted=False` — C is a dict class patched in place, not a replacement slotted type; (2) `added_ordering=True` — `_determine_attrs_eq_order(..., default_eq=True)` returned `(True, True)`, so C gets `__lt__/__le__/__gt__/__ge__`, whereas define resolved `(None, False)`; (3) `on_setattr_hook=None` — no convert+validate pipe, so converters/validators never re-run on assignment; (4) `collected_fields_by_mro=False` — base attributes would be gathered by the legacy, known-wrong `_collect_base_attrs_broken`, while define hard-codes `collect_by_mro=True`; (5) `added_pickling=False` — `getstate_setstate` defaults to `slots`, which is False, so no `__getstate__`/`__setstate__`; (6) `auto_detect=False` (and `auto_exc=False`), so hand-written dunders on the class are silently overwritten; and `force_kw_only` defaults to `True` (though with `kw_only` falsy it never fires here)."},{"id":"p8","answer":"Both `attrs.fields(C).a.type` and `C.__annotations__` are empty of type information: the `_CountingAttr`s made by bare `attrib()` carry no type, `_get_annotations(C)` returned `{}`, so the Attributes are built with `type=None`, and `make_class` sets `cls.__annotations__` from the fields' `type` values only after the build — producing `{}`. If you instead passed `{'a': field(type=int), ...}`, the field's type would be recorded on the `Attribute` and that post-build annotation step would populate `C.__annotations__` from those types (the documentation states the annotations are set from the fields' `type` values, and that they are deliberately set *after* the build so `_transform_attrs` doesn't mistake them for auto_attribs declarations); the exact resulting dict for the typed case isn't shown in the trace."},{"id":"g1","answer":"The guarantee is a clean retry: `define` runs the entire class build inside `try: do_it(cls, True) except UnannotatedAttributeError: do_it(cls, False)`, and that exception is raised in `_transform_attrs` at the very top of the build — before `_ClassBuilder` has written anything onto the class — so the second attempt sees the class exactly as the author wrote it. The silent-shrinkage case is the fallback itself: one bare `field()`/`attrib()` without an annotation makes the annotated attempt fail, and the retry with `auto_attribs=False` collects fields only from explicit `field()`/`attrib()` definitions (ordered by the `_CountingAttr` counter). Any plain annotated declarations such as `a_number: int = 42` are then not fields at all, and no error is raised. (A related silent effect documented elsewhere is ClassVar detection being textual — an unrecognized alias like `tp.ClassVar[int]` becomes a field instead of being skipped, which is the opposite direction.)"},{"id":"g2","answer":"The condition, checked once in `_ClassBuilder.__init__` on the non-frozen branch where `self._on_setattr in (_DEFAULT_ON_SETATTR, setters.validate, setters.convert)`: if `self._on_setattr == _DEFAULT_ON_SETATTR and not (has_validator or has_converter)` — i.e. the hook is exactly the default convert+validate pipe and no field declares a validator or converter — then `self._on_setattr = None`, and `add_setattr` subsequently writes no `__setattr__` at all. Two surprises: (1) introspection disagrees with behaviour — `ClassProps`/`attrs.inspect()` still report `on_setattr_hook=<wrapped_pipe>` even though nothing will run; (2) the decision is frozen at class-creation time, so attaching a validator or converter to an `Attribute` by hand afterwards has no effect, because the class has no `__setattr__` to invoke it. (A custom callable is never pruned — the shortcut recognizes only the three built-in hooks by equality.)"},{"id":"g3","answer":"The documentation covers only part of this. Preconditions: before any method is written, attrs reads `ClassProps.is_hashable` (true only for `Hashability.HASHABLE` or `HASHABLE_CACHED`) and rejects `cache_hash=True` on a non-hashable class with a `TypeError`; and in the `init=False` branch `cache_hash=True` is likewise rejected, since there would be nothing to initialize the cache. It also makes `needs_cached_setattr = cache_hash or frozen` true, so the generated `__init__` opens with `_setattr = _cached_setattr_get(self)` and appends a hash-cache line. The documentation does not name the attribute the cached hash is stored in, nor does it discuss any hazard involving `__attrs_post_init__` — I can't answer those parts from what I was given."},{"id":"g4","answer":"Only one case is documented in detail: in `define`'s `wrap`, attrs walks `cls.__bases__` looking for a base whose `__setattr__ is _frozen_setattrs`. If one is found, the subclass is treated as frozen and `on_setattr` is forced to `NO_OP` — but if the caller *also* passed an `on_setattr`, that combination raises instead, with the message \"Frozen classes can't use on_setattr (frozen-ness was inherited).\" The documentation quotes the message but does not state the exception class, and it does not describe the directly-frozen (`frozen=True` plus `on_setattr`) case or any other refusal, so I can't give those from this material."},{"id":"g5","answer":"Because `__slots__` can't be added after class creation, `_create_slots_class` builds a *new* type. It starts from a copy of the class dict with the field names, `__dict__` and `__weakref__` removed (so the class-body `42` and `Factory(list)` disappear); on 3.14+ it also clears the original type's descriptors. It walks the MRO for inherited slots and an existing `__weakref__`, appending a weakref slot if none exists; it slots only names not inherited from a base, and re-binds slots a base already defines from the collected descriptors so a parent's descriptor isn't shadowed by an empty one. A `functools.cached_property` gets its name slotted plus a generated `__getattr__` to compute and cache it. It sets `cd[\"__slots__\"]` and `cd[\"__qualname__\"]` and calls `type(cls)(cls.__name__, cls.__bases__, cd)`. Finally it walks the new class's dict — unwrapping classmethods, staticmethods and properties — and rewrites any closure cell still pointing at the discarded class (so `__class__`/bare `super()` keep working). `build_class` then records `__attrs_base_of_slotted__ = weakref.ref(cls)` and may call an inherited `__attrs_init_subclass__`. Consequences: the object bound to your class name is not the one the decorator received, `object.__init_subclass__` misbehaves, the dead original lingers in `type.__subclasses__` until a GC, pre-decoration references point at a dead class, and you should use `__attrs_init_subclass__` rather than `__init_subclass__`."},{"id":"g6","answer":"The documentation describes `fields` only. `fields(cls)` first asks `get_generic_base(cls)` whether the argument is a specialized generic alias like `A[str]` (for a plain class this returns `None`); if the argument is not a class it goes through an instance-handling branch; otherwise it returns `getattr(cls, \"__attrs_attrs__\", None)` — the generated `<Name>Attributes` tuple subclass, indexable and name-addressable. A non-class, non-instance argument raises `TypeError`, and a class without `__attrs_attrs__` raises `NotAnAttrsClassError`, both before any work is done. The documentation says nothing about `attrs.fields_dict`, and it does not describe any side effect of `fields` on generic aliases beyond consulting `get_generic_base` — so I can't answer the comparison or the side-effect part."},{"id":"g7","answer":"The generated `__repr__` opens by looking up `_compat.repr_context.already_repring`, a thread-local set of `id(self)` values; if this instance is already being repr'd somewhere up the stack it returns `'...'` instead of recursing forever (the script's `try:` / `alre…` prologue visible in the trace, with `AttributeError` in its globals). The thread-local deliberately lives in `_compat` rather than `_make` so the generated functions hold no direct reference to it — a direct reference would break cloudpickle."}]}
